narrative:
Your law-school application was denied because the model estimated a 55.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but it means the model judged failure more likely than passing, so your application did not clear the admission threshold.

The strongest factor increasing that concern was your plan to attend part-time. Accepted students in this dataset were overwhelmingly full-time, and part-time status was the single most influential feature pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. By contrast, the next two most important factors—your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA—both worked in your favor in the model. Your LSAT score of 33.50 is below the accepted-student average of 37.18, yet it still counted as a modest positive in this prediction. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30, slightly above the accepted average of 3.23, was another favorable factor. So the denial was driven mainly by the part-time study plan rather than by your academic record alone.

To strengthen a future application, consider whether you can reduce work hours or switch to full-time study, since that was the dominant concern. If feasible, retake the LSAT to raise your score, and provide any context that explains your preparation or circumstances. Speak with admissions counseling about how part-time applicants are evaluated, and consider programs or schedules that align with full-time study expectations. Reapply only after addressing the factor that most strongly increased the predicted risk.
